paras: The Coney Island attack on Black bathers was an attempted lynching in which a crowd of white bathers at Coney Island, New York, set upon two Black men, Bryant Teal and Frank Davis, in late July 1910 because they had entered the surf alongside white men and women. Davis was dragged into deep water, apparently to drown him, and Teal was chased under a hail of stones, but both escaped. Wire reports carried it in Southern papers as an attempt to lynch, while the Black press reprinted a New York editorial that ridiculed the attackers' claim to a "white man's ocean."

According to the New York dispatch, Teal and Davis put on bathing suits during the heat of the day and went into the water at the head of the pier, where about sixty white men and women were bathing. A German-language account placed them at the bathing place at the foot of Henderson's Walk and described Davis as Teal's friend.

Someone raised an outcry against the two men's presence. In the New York Globe's version, the bathers told them to go swimming in the Dead Sea, the Great Salt Lake or the Gowanus Canal, "but keep away from us." Several men then seized Davis, who was slightly built, and pulled him beyond his depth; the dispatch said "their object seemed to drown him." Davis proved a fast swimmer, struck out away from his attackers, made a wide detour to shore and ran for cover.

Teal, described as six feet tall and powerfully built, reached shore and fled under a hail of stones with the crowd behind him. Nearly winded, he was called into a small place of business by a white man, James Beaver, who stood off the crowd while Teal hid in the rear. Teal later slipped out a back window and made his way home, and the chase caused so much excitement that a dozen calls for police were sent in.
No report of an arrest, police inquiry or prosecution appears in the coverage.

The story reached readers mainly through a New York wire report that ran in small Southern weeklies in early August. The Mathews Journal in Virginia printed the long version with the men's names under the headline "Bathers at Coney Island Object to Their Presence in the Water," and the Bamberg Herald in South Carolina ran a shorter, unnamed telegram as "Negroes Threatened with Lynching." The Yorkville Enquirer gave it one sentence among unrelated news briefs.

Some white papers used the episode as commentary. The Pensacola Journal set the Northern mob against the South, remarking that "no one in the south objects to the negro trying to keep clean," in a column that also mocked the boxer Jack Johnson. Der Staats-Anzeiger of Rugby, North Dakota, headed its account "Black and white at the beach" and said Black people had seemed emboldened since the Black victory over a white fighter at Reno.

The Black press coverage found consists of a single editorial paragraph from the New York Globe, "White Man's Ocean," which the St. Paul Appeal printed on August 6 and again on September 24. The Globe mocked the "Caucasians of Coney Island" for objecting "violently" to Black bathers and then throwing the two men into the same Atlantic to "half drown them." It closed by calling the affair worth "a bitter laugh, with much of shame mixed in," a sharper judgment than any of the wire reports offered.

The Yorkville Enquirer, the Bamberg Herald's telegram and the Globe dated the attack to Friday, July 29, while the Mathews Journal's dispatch was datelined July 30 and the Pensacola Journal said "last Saturday" and spoke of only one man. Accounts of harm also differ: the wire reports describe stoning and an attempted drowning without stating injuries, whereas the Globe said the men were half drowned and the German report said both were beaten with slats and sticks before reaching Beaver's house.

reader.title: Coney Island attack on Black bathers (1910)
bases: White bathers at Coney Island seized one Black man and pulled him into deep water with, in the wire's words, the object of drowning him, and chased and stoned or beat both men; the wire reports call it an attempt to lynch, and no one was killed (A2, A3, A6).

Both men escaped alive, so the episode was an attempted lynching rather than a completed one (A2, A3, A1); the attackers were 'several men' and a crowd of bathers acting without authority, and the stated reason was the men's bathing alongside white men and women (A2, A4).

Two differently worded New York wire versions (A2, A3), the New York Globe editorial carried by the Black press (A4) and a German-language report with its own local detail (A6) agree that a crowd of white bathers attacked two Black men for bathing and that both escaped.

framing.detail: Headlines 'Negroes Threatened with Lynching' and 'Bathers at Coney Island Object to Their Presence in the Water'; the text calls it an attempt to lynch and says the attackers 'seemed to want his life'.
A one-line item among unrelated briefs in a South Carolina news column.
The Pensacola Journal set the Northern mob against the South, saying 'no one in the south objects to the negro trying to keep clean', next to a jibe at Jack Johnson.
The German-language paper headed it 'Black and white at the beach' and attributed the men's boldness to the Black victory at Reno.

The St. Paul Appeal reprinted the New York Globe's sardonic 'White Man's Ocean', mocking the attackers' inconsistency and ending on 'a bitter laugh, with much of shame mixed in', and ran it again seven weeks later.

The Pensacola Journal's later editorial brief is the only source for one victim.
